title: RSI, explained: Nvidia's lowest reading in almost 5 years #RSI #Nvidia #StockMarket #Shorts
description:
Search "Finance Toolkit MCP" to give your AI these numbers.

The relative strength index (RSI) compares a stock's average gains with its average losses over the last 14 trading days and scales them from 0 to 100: RSI = 100 − 100 ÷ (1 + average gain ÷ average loss). Below 30 is called oversold, above 70 overbought. At Thursday 5 November's close, after a 9.3% fall, Nvidia's RSI was 25.4, its lowest reading since at least November 2021 (12 closes below 30 in that time, the lowest before this 26.8 in January 2022). The S&P 500 stayed at 33.6 and Apple at 53.0; AMD was at 29.7 and TSMC at 26.5. The pitfall: oversold isn't cheap. On 25 January 2022 Nvidia's RSI was 26.8; by 14 October 2022 the price had fallen another 49.6%. RSI also shifts a little with how much history it's calculated on, so compare readings from the same source.

Read RSI as the speed of a move, not as what a company is worth.

title: Beta, explained: why Nvidia fell twice the market #Beta #StockMarket #Investing #Nvidia #Shorts
description:
Search "Finance Toolkit MCP" to give your AI these numbers.

Beta measures how far a stock tends to move when the market moves: the covariance of its daily returns with the market's, divided by the variance of the market's. The market itself has a beta of 1. On Thursday 5 November the S&P 500 closed 4.3% lower. Nvidia, with a 2026 beta of 1.82 against the S&P 500, fell 9.3%; beta alone pointed to about 7.9%. Coca-Cola, with a beta of −0.28, closed 0.1% lower. AMD (beta 3.34) fell 17.3% and Tesla (2.16) 10.8%. The pitfall: a low beta isn't low risk. Coca-Cola's price swung 19.7% a year in 2026, more than the S&P 500's 13.5%, just not in step with the market. Beta also shifts with the window: Nvidia's was 2.66 in 2024.

Multiply a stock's beta by the market's move to see the part that is the market; what's left is the company's own story.

title: KLM's 5,000 job cuts aren't the big number #KLM #AirFranceKLM #Airlines #Investing #Stocks #Shorts
description:

KLM said on 5 November that about 5,000 positions will be cut, outsourced or transferred, close to 15% of its workforce. Most move to other employers rather than disappear; outlets put the outright eliminations at about 1,000. The bigger number is the goal: a €1 billion yearly improvement by 2028, about half of Air France-KLM's 2025 operating profit of €2.0 billion. At 17:02 Amsterdam the shares were up 13% while Lufthansa was up 0.3%. The group keeps 6.2% of its revenue as operating profit; IAG, the owner of British Airways, keeps 14.7%. Even the full €1 billion, at 2025 revenue, would lift that to about 9%.

Judge a cost cut against operating profit, not the job count.

title: S&P 500 rose 1.8% after the midterms but it's sectors depict a different story.  #investing
description:

The day after the 3 November US midterm elections, the S&P 500 was up 1.8% at 1:30 pm New York. Underneath, consumer discretionary rose 4.6% and energy fell 5.0%, a gap of almost ten percentage points in one session. Since 30 September the index is barely changed, though nine of the eleven sectors rose: technology, its largest part, fell 9.5%. In all 19 midterm years since 1950 the S&P 500 was higher twelve months later; a small sample, not a forecast.

An index is an average. Split it into its sectors to see what the market is pricing.

title: Gold fell 27% from its peak. Its worst fall since 1980 was 70% #trading #investing #financetoolkit
description:
Sarch "Finance Toolkit MCP" to give your AI these numbers.

Gold settled at its lowest price in a year on 30 October ($3,898.90 on Comex, MarketWatch). That was 27% below its 2026 peak close.

Since 1980, three of its falls were deeper than this one: 70% from January 1980 to July 1999, 30% in 2008, and 45% from 2011 to 2015. It took until November 2007, almost 28 years, to get back above the 1980 peak. The S&P 500's deepest fall since 1980 was 57% (October 2007 to March 2009), not as deep as gold's.

For gold, or anything seen as safe, the deepest fall in its own history (its maximum drawdown) says more about its risk than its reputation does. The same check works for any fund, stock or currency. Long-term US Treasuries, another asset seen as safe, fell 49% from August 2020 to October 2023 (TLT, interest included).
